nodes.label: US rationing 1917–18
nodes.full: America rations sugar in the war and saves 775,000 tons.

nodes.label: Beet subsidy and Tate & Lyle
nodes.full: Britain subsidises home beet from 1921; Tate and Lyle is formed.

nodes.label: Graves’s tea
nodes.full: Graves’s first meal at the front is bread, bacon, rum and sugared tea.

nodes.label: Second World War
nodes.full: U-boats and rationing, 1939–45.

nodes.label: British rationing
nodes.full: Sugar is rationed in Britain 1940–53.

nodes.label: Kathleen Hey’s diary
nodes.full: A Dewsbury shop assistant records the ration cut.

nodes.label: Tate not State
nodes.full: Labour’s plan to nationalise sugar is beaten off.

nodes.label: Mr Cube
nodes.full: Mr Cube becomes the face of sugar.

nodes.label: Britain 1921–38
nodes.full: British homes eat 1.1 million tons of sugar by 1938.

nodes.label: Biscuits and chocolate
nodes.full: Biscuit and chocolate factories use sugar by the ton.

nodes.full: British consumption peaks at 115 lb a head in 1958.

nodes.full: Nutrition science finds sugar devoid of vitamins and minerals.

nodes.full: School dentists find children’s teeth corroded by sugar.

nodes.label: Yudkin 1957
nodes.full: Yudkin reports sugar in the international heart-disease statistics.

nodes.label: Harvard review 1967
nodes.full: The sugar industry pays Harvard scientists to blame fat.

nodes.label: The glut
nodes.full: A glut of overproduction in 1900–14 breaks smallholder cane.

nodes.label: Brussels 1902
nodes.full: The Brussels Convention tries to end beet bounties.

nodes.label: Chadbourne 1931
nodes.full: The Chadbourne Agreement tries to restrict world output.

nodes.label: Tenfold yields

nodes.label: Hong Kong refineries
nodes.full: Hong Kong refineries undercut the Pearl River Delta.

nodes.label: Hong Kong’s supplies
nodes.full: Hong Kong’s refiners buy from Java and the Philippines.

nodes.label: Taiwan’s sugar rules
nodes.full: Japan’s 1902 rules turn Taiwan into another Java.

nodes.label: Taiwan’s land
nodes.full: Five Japanese firms own 70% of Taiwan’s cane land.

nodes.label: Rose Bamboo
nodes.full: Taiwan’s Rose Bamboo cane and steam mills.

nodes.label: Taiwan irrigation
nodes.full: The Chia-i–Tainan irrigation system serves 370,500 acres.

nodes.label: Taiwan’s cane farmers
nodes.full: Taiwan’s cane farmers under company contract.

nodes.label: Taiwan to Japan
nodes.full: Taiwan sells to Japan under preferential tariffs.

nodes.label: Cuba 1902–25
nodes.full: Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic make 6.75 million tons by 1923.

nodes.label: Cuba after 1929
nodes.full: The crash brings unrest and revolution to Cuba.

nodes.label: US Sugar Act 1937
nodes.full: The 1937 Sugar Act regiments the sugar market.

nodes.label: Cuba and USSR
nodes.full: Cuba turns to the Soviet Union for its sugar market.

nodes.label: Florida sugar
nodes.full: Florida sugar grows from 29,000 tons in 1934 to nearly a million in the mid-1960s.

nodes.label: Guest workers
nodes.full: West Indian and Mexican guest workers cut Florida’s cane.

nodes.label: Everglades

nodes.full: C&H Sugar and the American Sugar Refining Company, 1906–07.

nodes.label: Hawaii a territory

nodes.label: Coke abroad
nodes.full: Coca-Cola spreads abroad with aid-funded plants.

nodes.full: Saccharin goes on sale in the war of 1914.

nodes.full: The Marshall Plan sends Europe American food.

edges: Walvin: within days of war being declared in 1914 Britain founded a Royal Commission for Sugar Supplies.
Graves’s first meal at the front is Walvin’s illustration of the sugar and rum that fed the army.
Walvin: wartime state support for beet and refiners was extended from 1921 with the promotion of the British beet industry.
Walvin sets the American wartime sugar controls of 1917–18 beside the British problem of lost German beet.
Walvin: with state support and the beet subsidy, Tate and Lyle and a few refiners became powerful and British consumption grew through to 1938.
Walvin: sweets, chocolate, biscuits and jam took a large share of the sugar eaten by the British.
Walvin: sugar was rationed in Britain at 12 oz a week from January 1940 because of the loss of beet and the submarine war.
Hey’s diary shows how the cuts of the ration were felt.
Walvin: the wartime state system was hard to dismantle, and Labour then put sugar on its list for nationalisation.
Walvin: ‘Mr Cube’ was the icon of Tate and Lyle’s campaign against nationalisation.
Walvin: after rationing, British consumption rose to 115 lb a head in 1958.
Walvin: the new nutrition science and school dentists found sugar devoid of vitamins and harmful to children’s teeth.
Yudkin writes that Keys’s fat idea was the context for his own 1957 suggestion that sugar be examined.
Walvin: critics of sugar began to be heard in the 1960s, and the industry-sponsored 1967 review moved the blame to fat; Yudkin’s sugar researches were belittled.
Walvin: the 1967 review pushed the blame for heart disease onto fat, the Keys position.
Mazumdar’s glut of 1900–14 and the Brussels Convention of 1902 against bounties belong to the same crisis of overproduction.
The 1931 Chadbourne Agreement followed the breakdown of the 1902 convention, according to the web summary.
Mazumdar: the tenfold rise in sugar per acre between 1850 and 1950 contributed to the glut and the price slump.
Mazumdar: the slump in world prices is what brought Hong Kong’s refined sugar to China at lower prices.
Mazumdar: by 1900–10 the Hong Kong refineries got all their raw stocks from Java and the Philippines.
Mazumdar: the crisis of overproduction was the world setting in which Taiwan’s industrial sugar was built.
Mazumdar: the 1902 regulations and the 1905 ban on buffalo mills were the tools by which Taiwan’s industry was built.
Mazumdar: the Taiwan Seito Kaisha mill began in 1901 and the Rose Bamboo variety spread by police distribution.
Mazumdar: the irrigation of the 1920s served the rotation of cane and rice that the earlier mills depended on.
Mazumdar: the folk song of the 1920s describes the cane farmers whom the company contracts bound to the mills.
Mazumdar: Taiwan’s status as a colony gave it a preferential tariff for exports to Japan.
Walvin: Cuba’s output, tied to US capital, was hit by the crash of 1929.
Walvin: Roosevelt’s sugar quota compromise was worked out to deal with the danger of upheaval in Cuba.
Walvin: the 1937 quota system was dismantled when Congress cut Cuba’s quota after the revolution.
Walvin: after Castro confiscated the estates Congress cut Cuba’s quota.
Walvin: with its quota slashed, Cuba turned to Russia and Eastern Europe, and Kennedy banned all trade.
Walvin: the cut in Cuba’s quota gave American growers the green light that led to Florida’s sugar rush.
Walvin: Florida’s cane-cutting relied on 20,000 West Indian guest workers a year by the mid-1960s.
Smith and Walvin: Florida’s sugar expanded on the drained land of the Everglades.
Walvin and Smith: Hawaii’s status as a US territory in 1900 and C&H Sugar from 1906 gave it free access to the mainland market.
Coca-Cola, the largest industrial user of sugar by 1910, doubled its sales with the US military in the war.
Walvin: after the war Coca-Cola spread overseas with US aid and plants, over forty new in 1960.
Walvin ties Coca-Cola’s postwar growth to McDonald’s and the other fast-food chains.
Walvin: after saccharin and cyclamate, the corn-based HFCS of 1957 was the next sweetener to transform soft drinks.
Yudkin: HFCS use rose from 3 to 43 lb a head in the US between 1974 and 1983, almost all in food manufacture.
Yudkin and Walvin: the move of sugar use from kitchen to factory is the same shift as the rise of supermarket convenience foods.
Walvin: sweet children’s cereal and ‘Just heat and serve’ foods belong to the same postwar industrial food culture.
Walvin: the Marshall Plan and European agricultural resolve form the setting of the postwar industrial food system.
In Iran and Turkey in the 1930s the state, not private planters, drove the new sugar economy — taxes on sugar and tea in one, state sugar plants in the other.
Turkey’s plants of 1934–38 and Egypt’s protected industries of the 1930s are the same post-depression pattern of state-promoted import substitution in this atlas.
